description: Article-based learning cards with subtitle, body paragraphs, and takeaway.

cards.title: Every Company Is Now a Software Company
cards.subtitle: The bookstore became a cloud giant. The taxi company doesn't own cars.
body: Amazon started selling books. Now it runs a third of the internet. Uber disrupted transportation without owning a single vehicle.
The winners aren't those with the most physical assets—they're the ones with the best software.
cards.takeaway: Software transforms industries by replacing physical assets with code.

cards.title: Why Now? The Infrastructure Exists
cards.subtitle: Six decades of progress created the foundation.
body:
• Broadband reaches billions
• Smartphones in every pocket
• Cloud computing for pennies
None of this existed twenty years ago. The pieces had to come together first.
cards.takeaway: Software is eating the world now because the infrastructure finally supports it.

cards.title: Retail Was the First Meal
cards.subtitle: Borders went bankrupt. Amazon is worth over a trillion.
body: Physical retail required real estate and staff in every location. E-commerce required a website and a warehouse.
One scaled linearly with geography. The other scaled with servers.
cards.takeaway: Software-based businesses have fundamentally different—and better—economics.

cards.title: Entertainment Got Eaten Next
cards.subtitle: Blockbuster had 9,000 stores. Netflix has an algorithm.
body: Video rental required physical locations and inventory. Streaming requires bandwidth and a monthly fee.
Netflix didn't just replace Blockbuster—it redefined what's possible.
cards.takeaway: Software doesn't just compete with incumbents—it redefines the industry.

cards.title: Music Was Disrupted Twice
cards.subtitle: Napster broke it. Apple rebuilt it. Spotify ate Apple's model.
body: The music industry fought piracy while software companies figured out how to monetize convenience.
People didn't want to own songs—they wanted access to everything for $10/month.
cards.takeaway: Incumbents rarely disrupt themselves—software companies do it for them.

cards.title: Gaming Became Bigger Than Movies
cards.subtitle: Video games now generate more revenue than film and music combined.
body: Games went from arcades to consoles to phones. Each transition expanded the market exponentially.
Fortnite generates billions with no physical distribution, no inventory, no retail.
cards.takeaway: Software-native entertainment formats outgrew traditional media.

cards.title: Telecom Is Becoming Software
cards.subtitle: Skype let you call anyone for free. Phone companies never recovered.
body: Voice calls used to require massive infrastructure. Then software turned voice into data packets.
WhatsApp: acquired for $19B with 55 employees. Traditional telecoms: hundreds of thousands.
cards.takeaway: When communication becomes software, old infrastructure becomes a liability.

cards.title: Cars Are Computers on Wheels
cards.subtitle: Tesla's value isn't in the factory. It's in the code.
body: A modern car runs on millions of lines of code—braking, entertainment, autonomous driving.

• Tesla ships updates overnight
• Traditional automakers ship new models every few years
cards.takeaway: Even hardware-heavy industries are being redefined by software.

cards.title: Healthcare Is Next
cards.subtitle: Your medical records are still faxed. That's about to change.
body: Healthcare resisted software transformation—regulation and entrenched interests slowed adoption.
But telemedicine, AI diagnostics, and digital records are creating cracks in the old system.
cards.takeaway: Regulation can delay software disruption but not prevent it.

cards.title: Education Is Overdue
cards.subtitle: The lecture format hasn't changed in 500 years.
body: Universities operate on scarcity—limited seats, limited professors, geographic constraints.
Online courses reach millions. AI tutors personalize at scale. The economics favor software.
cards.takeaway: Education's business model is vulnerable; only credentialing has protected it.

cards.title: The Talent War Is Real
cards.subtitle: Every company needs engineers. There aren't enough.
body: If software is eating every industry, software talent is the scarcest resource.
The best engineers choose where they work. This is why tech compensation has diverged.
cards.takeaway: The people who build software have leverage because everyone needs them.

cards.title: Investors Finally Understand
cards.subtitle: Software companies are now the most valuable on earth.
body: In 2011, people doubted software could build durable businesses. Now the top 5 companies are all software-driven.
The thesis wasn't wrong—it was early.
cards.takeaway: Software's dominance is no longer a prediction. It's the observable reality.
